1      THIS MATTER comes before the Court on motions1 to consolidate, appoint lead 
2  plaintiff, and approve lead counsel brought by (i) Movant Lee McCormick, docket 
3  no. 17, (ii) Movant Alex Ambrose, docket no. 20, (iii) Movant Joseph Switzer, docket 

4  no. 24, (iv) Movant Jeremy Jaeger, docket no. 26, (v) Movant Steven Hackbarth, docket 
5  no. 31, (vi) Movant Slav Danev, docket no. 33, and (vii) Movant Sjunde AP-Fonden 
6  (“AP7”), docket no. 34.2  Having reviewed all papers filed in support of, and in 
7  opposition to, the motions, and having concluded that oral argument is unnecessary, the 
8  Court enters the following Order.                                        

9  Background                                                               
10      Zillow Group, Inc. (“Zillow”) is a real estate services company.  Compl. at ¶ 2 
11  (C21-1551 TSZ, docket no. 1).  “Zillow Offers” is Zillow’s “home-flipping” business, 
12  through which Zillow “directly purchases homes from sellers, makes certain repairs and 
13  updates to these properties, and subsequently resells the homes to purchasers.”  Compl. at 

14  ¶ 2 (C22-14 TSZ, docket no. 1).                                          
15      On November 16, 2021, Zillow shareholder Dibakar Barua filed a putative class 
16  action against Zillow and individual defendants Richard Barton, Allen Parker, and 
17  Jeremy Wacksman, alleging claims under Sections 10(b) and 20(a) of the Securities 
18  Exchange Act of 1934 (the “Exchange Act”), as well as Rule 10b-5, which was 

19  promulgated by the United States Securities and Exchange Commission.  See Compl. at 
20                                                                           
21  1 The pending motions were filed in the Barua action, No. C21-1551 TSZ.  
  2 A similar motion brought by movant Slav Danev, docket no. 27, has been withdrawn.  See Notice of 
22  Withdrawal (docket no. 40).                                              
1  ¶¶ 54–68 (C21-1551 TSZ).  On November 19, 2021, shareholder Steven Silverberg filed 
2  a second putative class action against Zillow and individual defendants Richard Barton, 
3  Allen Parker, and Jeremy Wacksman, alleging the same claims under the Exchange Act.  

4  Compl. at ¶¶ 54–68 (C21-1567 TSZ, docket no. 1).  On January 6, 2022, Zillow 
5  shareholder Aaron Hillier filed a third putative class action against Zillow and individual 
6  defendants Richard Barton, Allen Parker, Lloyd Frink, and Jeremy Wacksman, also 
7  alleging the same violations of the Exchange Act.  Compl. at ¶¶ 63–70 (C22-14 TSZ).   
8      Multiple parties, all Zillow shareholders, now move the Court to consolidate the 

9  Barua, Silverberg, and Hillier actions and appoint lead plaintiff and counsel.  See 
10  C21-1551 TSZ, docket nos. 17, 20, 24, 26, 31, 33 and 34.  The Movants are shareholders 
11  Lee McCormick, Alex Ambrose, Joseph Switzer, Jeremy Jaeger, Steven Hackbarth, Slav 
12  Danev, and AP7.  As discussed below, the Court concludes that consolidation is 
13  appropriate and appoints Movant Jeremy Jaeger as lead plaintiff.         

14      As required by the Private Securities Litigation Reform Act (“PSLRA”), all named 
15  plaintiffs and all movants seeking appointment as lead plaintiff have filed the requisite 
16  certifications.3  See Ex. 1 to Compl. (C21-1551 TSZ, docket no. 1-1) (Barua Certif.); 
17  Attach. 1 to Compl. (C21-1567 TSZ, docket no. 1-1) (Silverberg Certif.); Compl. (C22-
18  14 TSZ, docket no. 1 at 23–24) (Hillier Certif.); Ex. B to Nivison Decl. (C21-1551 TSZ,

  counsel or in order to participate in the action and that the plaintiff will not accept any payment for 
21                                                                           
  serving as the class representative beyond the plaintiff’s pro rata share of any recovery, except for 
  reasonable costs and expenses (including lost wages) directly related to the representation of the class.  
22  See 15 U.S.C. §§ 78u-4(a)(2)&(4).                                        
1  docket no. 18-2) (McCormick Certif.); Ex. A to Townsend Decl. (docket no. 21-1) 
2  (Ambrose Certif.); Ex. A to Stephens Decl. (docket no. 25-1) (Switzer Certif.); Ex. A to 
3  Berman Decl. (docket no. 28-1) (Jaeger Certif.); Ex. C to Lieberman Decl. (docket no. 

4  32-3) (Hackbarth Certif.); Ex. B to Phillips Decl. (docket no. 33-3) (Danev Certif.); Ex. A 
5  to Keller Decl. (docket no. 35 at 6–9) (AP7 Certif.).  In accordance with the PSLRA, on 
6  November 16, 2021, plaintiff Barua arranged for notice of his lawsuit to be filed.  See Ex. 
7  D to Berman Decl. (docket no. 28-4); 15 U.S.C. § 78u-4(a)(3)(A)(i).  The pending 
8  motions to appoint lead plaintiff were timely filed.                     

9  Discussion                                                               
10      1.   Consolidation of Related Cases                                  
11      A district court may consolidate actions that involve common questions of law or 
12  fact.  Fed. R. Civ. P. 42(a).  Under the PSLRA, “[i]f more than one action on behalf of a 
13  class asserting substantially the same claim or claims . . . has been filed, and any party 

14  has sought to consolidate those actions,” a court must determine whether to consolidate 
15  the actions before appointing a lead plaintiff.  15 U.S.C. § 78u-4(a)(3)(B)(ii).   
16      The Barua, Silverberg, and Hillier actions are almost identical.4  The three actions 
17  allege that Defendants artificially inflated the price of Zillow securities by making 
18  materially false and/or misleading statements and by failing to disclose material adverse 

19                                                                           

20                                                                           
  4 The Hillier action proposes a longer class period (August 7, 2020 through November 2, 2021) than the 
  Barua and Silverberg actions (February 10, 2021 through November 2, 2021).  Compare Compl. at ¶ 1 
21                                                                           
  (C22-14 TSZ), with Compl. at ¶ 1 (C21-1551 TSZ), and Compl. at ¶ 1 (C21-1567 TSZ).  The Hillier 
  action also brings its claims under the Exchange Act against an additional defendant, Lloyd Frink, 
22  Zillow’s President and Executive Chairman.  Compl. at ¶ 15 (C22-14 TSZ). 
1  facts about Zillow Offers.  See Compl. at ¶¶ 54–68 (C21-1551 TSZ); Compl. at ¶¶ 54–68 
2  (C21-1567 TSZ); Compl. at ¶¶ 63–70 (C22-14 TSZ).  All Movants request that the Court 
3  consolidate the above-captioned cases.  See C21-1551 TSZ, dockets nos. 17, 20, 24, 26, 

4  31, 33 & 34.  Defendants do not oppose consolidation.  See Resp. (docket no. 52). 
5      Therefore, the Court finds that the Barua, Silverberg, and Hillier actions share 
6  common questions of law and fact and that it is appropriate to consolidate these matters 
7  for all purposes.  The Movants’ motions to consolidate, docket nos. 17, 20, 24, 26, 31, 33 
8  and 34, are GRANTED.                                                     

9      2.   Appointment of Lead Plaintiff                                   
10      Having consolidated the Barua, Silverberg, and Hillier actions, the Court now 
11  considers the various motions to appoint a lead plaintiff.  The PSLRA sets forth a “simple 
12  three-step process for identifying” a lead plaintiff.  See In re Cavanaugh, 306 F.3d 726, 
13  729 (9th Cir. 2002).  The first step involves posting notice in a “widely circulated 

14  national business-oriented publication or wire service.”  Id. (citing 15 U.S.C. § 78u-
15  4(a)(3)(A)(i)).  This task has been performed.  In the second phase, the Court must select 
16  as the presumptively “most adequate plaintiff” the putative class member who (i) has 
17  filed a complaint or made a motion for appointment, (ii) has “the largest financial interest 
18  in the relief sought by the class,” and (iii) “otherwise satisfies the requirements of Rule 

19  23 of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure.”  See id. at 729–30; see also 15 U.S.C. 
20  § 78u-4(a)(3)(B)(iii)(I).  For purposes of appointing a lead plaintiff pursuant to the
21  PSLRA, the Court’s Rule 23 inquiry “is not as searching as it would be on a motion for 
22  class certification.”  See In re Outerwall Inc. S’holder Litig., No. C16-1275, 2017 WL 
1  881382, at *4 (W.D. Wash. Mar. 6, 2017).  During the third stage, others are given an 
2  opportunity to attempt to rebut the presumption that the selected putative class member is 
3  the “most adequate plaintiff” by offering proof that the selected member “is subject to 

4  unique defenses” or is otherwise incapable of “fairly and adequately” representing the 
5  class.  See Cavanaugh, 306 F.3d at 730; see also 15 U.S.C. § 78u-4(a)(3)(B)(iii)(II). 
6      Here, the parties do not dispute the relative losses alleged.  With $6,305,231.59 in 
7  estimated losses, Movant Jeremy Jaeger has the largest financial interest.  See Ex. B to 
8  Berman Decl. (docket no. 28-2).5  For comparison, the movant with the second largest 

9  estimated losses, $4,792,919.20, is AP7.  Ex. B to Keller Decl. (docket no. 35).  See 
10  Outerwall, 2017 WL 881382, at *4 (outlining four factors generally considered by 
11  courts); see also Lewis v. CytoDyn, Inc., No. C21-5190, 2021 WL 3709291, at *3–4 
12  (W.D. Wash. Aug. 19, 2021) (describing the same four factors, observing that the 
13  “trend among courts nationwide has been to use LIFO [last in, first out] in calculating 

14  competing movants’ estimated losses,” and explaining that the assumption under LIFO is 
15  the first stocks to be sold are the stocks most recently purchased).     
16      Jaeger has the largest financial interest and satisfies the requirements of Rule 23 in 
17  that Jaeger’s claims are typical of those of the class and Jaeger can be expected to fairly 
18  and adequately protect the interests of the class.  Cavanaugh, 306 F.3d at 730 (citing Fed. 

19  R. Civ. P. 23(a)); Lewis, 2021 WL 3709291, at *6 (typicality is shown if the proposed
20                                                                           
21                                                                           
  5 Jeremy Jaeger is not a named plaintiff in the above-captioned cases.  He is a Zillow shareholder who 
  filed a motion, docket no. 26, in the Barua action, C21-1551 TSZ, for appointment as lead plaintiff under 
22  the PSLRA.                                                               
1  lead plaintiff’s claims arise from the same event or course of conduct and are founded on 
2  the same legal theory as the class claims, and adequacy is established if the proposed lead 
3  plaintiff does not have any conflicts of interest with other class members and will, along 

4  with counsel, vigorously litigate on the class’s behalf); see also Jaeger Decl. at ¶¶ 2–7, 
5  Ex. C to Berman Decl. (docket no. 28-3) (explaining that Jaeger works as the president of 
6  a general engineering company, suffered substantial losses while trading Zillow securities 
7  during the class period, is strongly motivated to litigate vigorously and efficiently to 
8  maximize the recovery for himself and the putative class, and understands the important 

9  role of a lead plaintiff).  Accordingly, Jaeger is the presumptively “most adequate 
10  plaintiff.”                                                              
11      The remaining Movants do not oppose Jaeger’s appointment as lead plaintiff.  
12  Switzer, Hackbarth, Danev, and AP7 filed notices of non-opposition, docket nos. 50, 45, 
13  41, and 49, respectively.  The Court treats these Movants’ notices of non-opposition as 

14  withdrawal of their motions for appointment as lead plaintiff.  Therefore, Switzer, 
15  Hackbarth, Danev, and AP7’s motions, docket nos. 24, 31, 33, and 34, are STRICKEN in 
16  part as moot.                                                            
17      McCormick filed a response, docket no. 51, conceding that he does not possess the 
18  largest financial interest and requesting that the Court appoint him as lead plaintiff if the 

19  other Movants are disqualified.  The Court treats McCormick’s response as a notice of 
20  non-opposition, and McCormick’s motion, docket no. 17, is STRICKEN in part as moot.   
21      Ambrose initially challenged Jaeger’s financial interest, see docket no. 53, but 
22  later filed a notice of non-opposition to Jaeger’s appointment, docket no. 55.  Ambrose 
1  no longer questions Jaeger’s estimated losses, but requests that the Court appoint him as 
2  co-lead plaintiff alongside Jaeger because Jaeger traded exclusively in non-voting Class 
3  C shares while he traded in voting Class A shares.  See Notice of Non-Opp’n (docket 

4  no. 55 at 3).  The claims brought against Defendants and the nature of the putative class 
5  members’ alleged damages do not support Ambrose’s request that the Court appoint co-
6  lead plaintiffs.  See Outerwall, 2017 WL 881382, at *9 (“[T]he decision whether to 
7  appoint a co-lead plaintiff often turns on the existence of disparate sub-groups of 
8  plaintiffs in the putative class.”); Miller v. Ventro Corp., No. C01-01287, 2001 U.S. Dist. 

9  LEXIS 26027, at *33–38 (N.D. Cal. Nov. 28, 2001) (appointing co-lead plaintiffs to 
10  represent shareholders and bondholders when bondholders presented additional legal 
11  theories); In re CTI BioPharma Corp. Sec. Litig., No. C16-216, 2016 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 
12  119301, at *12 (W.D. Wash. Sept. 2, 2016) (declining to appoint co-lead plaintiffs for 
13  preferred and common stock); In re Juniper Networks, Inc. Sec. Litig., 264 F.R.D. 584, 

14  594 (N.D. Cal. 2009) (finding that courts regularly appoint purchasers of one type of 
15  security to represent purchasers of other types of securities when the purchasers’ interests 
16  align).                                                                  
17      Ambrose contends that Jaeger’s ownership of Class C shares might affect Jaeger’s 
18  decision-making at settlement or trial.  However, Ambrose’s speculation concerning 

19  Jaeger’s decision-making is insufficient.  Ambrose has not shown that Jaeger’s interests 
20  are separate or independent of the other shareholders’ interests.  All Movants raise the 
21  same claims against Defendants under the Exchange Act, and all allege that they suffered 
22  damages when Zillow’s stock price fell, regardless of whether their shares have voting 
1  rights.  Although Ambrose argues that Jaeger’s ownership of non-voting Class C shares 
2  might cause Jaeger to favor Class C shares over Class A shares, Ambrose has not 
3  established that the differences between Class A and C shares would affect the claims or 

4  damages in this case.  The Court concludes, therefore, that appointing co-lead plaintiffs is 
5  not necessary, and Ambrose’s motion, docket no. 20, is DENIED in part.   
6      Finally, the Movants have provided no reason to disturb Jaeger’s choice of 
7  counsel.  See 15 U.S.C. § 78u-4(a)(3)(B)(v) (“The most adequate plaintiff shall, subject 
8  to the approval of the court, select and retain counsel to represent the class.”); see also 

9  Cavanaugh, 306 F.3d at 734 (“While the appointment of counsel is made subject to the 
10  approval of the court, the [PSLRA] clearly leaves the choice of class counsel in the hands 
11  of the lead plaintiff.”).  Jaeger has selected Hagens Berman Sobol Shapiro LLP (“Hagens 
12  Berman”) as lead counsel.  Having reviewed the firm’s résumé, Ex. E to Berman Decl. 
13  (docket no. 28-5), the Court finds that Hagens Berman is qualified and experienced to 

14  serve as lead counsel for the putative class.  Thus, the Court approves Jaeger’s choice of 
15  lead counsel.                                                            
16  Conclusion                                                               
17      For the foregoing reasons, the Court ORDERS:                         
18      (1)  The Movants’ motions to consolidate, docket nos. 17, 20, 24, 26, 31, 33 and

19  34, are GRANTED.  The above-captioned Barua, Silverberg, and Hillier actions are 
20  hereby CONSOLIDATED for all purposes.  All future pleadings, motions, briefs, and 
21  other papers shall be filed only in Case No. C21-1551 TSZ.  The Clerk is DIRECTED to 
22  CLOSE Case Nos. C21-1567 TSZ and C22-14 TSZ;                             
1      (2)  Switzer’s motion, docket no. 24, Hackbarth’s motion, docket no. 31,
2  Danev’s motion, docket no. 33, AP7’s motion, docket no. 34, and McCormick’s motion, 
3  docket no. 17, are STRICKEN in part as moot;                             

4      (3)  Ambrose’s motion, docket no. 20, is DENIED as it relates to appointment
5  of co-lead plaintiffs;                                                   
6      (4)  Jaeger’s motion, docket no. 26, is GRANTED;                     
7      (5)  Jaeger is appointed lead plaintiff.  Jaeger’s choice of counsel is approved,
8  and Hagens Berman Sobol Shapiro LLP is appointed as lead counsel;        

9      (6)  Within fourteen (14) days of the date of this Order, lead plaintiff and
10  Defendants shall meet and confer and file a Joint Status Report proposing a schedule for 
11  this matter, including deadlines for the filing of a consolidated complaint and any 
12  responsive pleading or motion.  The Joint Status Report shall also identify one attorney 
13  from Hagens Berman Sobol Shapiro LLP, and one attorney for Defendants who shall 

14  serve as the liaison lawyer for each side; the liaison lawyers will have responsibility for 
15  receiving and, as appropriate, distributing to co-counsel any written or oral 
16  communications of the Court and serving as the contact point between the Court and all 
17  counsel to assist with scheduling and coordinating hearings and telephonic conferences; 
18  and                                                                      

19      (7)  The Clerk is directed to send a copy of this Order to all counsel of record.
20                                                                           
21                                                                           
22                                                                           
1      IT IS SO ORDERED.                                                    
2      Dated this 16th day of February, 2022.                               
3                                      A                                    

4                                    Thomas S. Zilly                        
                                     United States District Judge

4  31, 33 & 34.  Defendants do not oppose consolidation.  See Resp. (docket no. 52). 
5      Therefore, the Court finds that the Barua, Silverberg, and Hillier actions share 
6  common questions of law and fact and that it is appropriate to consolidate these matters 
7  for all purposes.  The Movants’ motions to consolidate, docket nos. 17, 20, 24, 26, 31, 33 
8  and 34, are GRANTED.                                                     

9      2.   Appointment of Lead Plaintiff                                   
10      Having consolidated the Barua, Silverberg, and Hillier actions, the Court now 
11  considers the various motions to appoint a lead plaintiff.  The PSLRA sets forth a “simple 
12  three-step process for identifying” a lead plaintiff.  See In re Cavanaugh,
306 F.3d 726
, 
13  729 (9th Cir. 2002).  The first step involves posting notice in a “widely circulated 

14  national business-oriented publication or wire service.”  Id. (citing 15 U.S.C. § 78u-
15  4(a)(3)(A)(i)).  This task has been performed.  In the second phase, the Court must select 
16  as the presumptively “most adequate plaintiff” the putative class member who (i) has 
17  filed a complaint or made a motion for appointment, (ii) has “the largest financial interest 
18  in the relief sought by the class,” and (iii) “otherwise satisfies the requirements of Rule 

19  23 of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure.”  See id. at 729–30; see also 15 U.S.C. 
20  § 78u-4(a)(3)(B)(iii)(I).  For purposes of appointing a lead plaintiff pursuant to the
21  PSLRA, the Court’s Rule 23 inquiry “is not as searching as it would be on a motion for 
22  class certification.”  See In re Outerwall Inc. S’holder Litig., No. C16-1275,
2017 WL 1
  881382, at *4 (W.D. Wash. Mar. 6, 2017).  During the third stage, others are given an 
2  opportunity to attempt to rebut the presumption that the selected putative class member is 
3  the “most adequate plaintiff” by offering proof that the selected member “is subject to 

4  unique defenses” or is otherwise incapable of “fairly and adequately” representing the 
5  class.  See Cavanaugh, 306 F.3d at 730; see also 15 U.S.C. § 78u-4(a)(3)(B)(iii)(II). 
6      Here, the parties do not dispute the relative losses alleged.  With $6,305,231.59 in 
7  estimated losses, Movant Jeremy Jaeger has the largest financial interest.  See Ex. B to 
8  Berman Decl. (docket no. 28-2).5  For comparison, the movant with the second largest 

9  estimated losses, $4,792,919.20, is AP7.  Ex. B to Keller Decl. (docket no. 35).  See 
10  Outerwall,
2017 WL 881382
, at *4 (outlining four factors generally considered by 
11  courts); see also Lewis v. CytoDyn, Inc., No. C21-5190,
2021 WL 3709291
, at *3–4 
12  (W.D. Wash. Aug. 19, 2021) (describing the same four factors, observing that the 
13  “trend among courts nationwide has been to use LIFO [last in, first out] in calculating 

14  competing movants’ estimated losses,” and explaining that the assumption under LIFO is 
15  the first stocks to be sold are the stocks most recently purchased).     
16      Jaeger has the largest financial interest and satisfies the requirements of Rule 23 in 
17  that Jaeger’s claims are typical of those of the class and Jaeger can be expected to fairly 
18  and adequately protect the interests of the class.  Cavanaugh, 306 F.3d at 730 (citing Fed. 

19  R. Civ. P. 23(a)); Lewis,
2021 WL 3709291
, at *6 (typicality is shown if the proposed
20                                                                           
21

  filed a motion, docket no. 26, in the Barua action, C21-1551 TSZ, for appointment as lead plaintiff under 
22  the PSLRA.                                                               
1  lead plaintiff’s claims arise from the same event or course of conduct and are founded on 
2  the same legal theory as the class claims, and adequacy is established if the proposed lead 
3  plaintiff does not have any conflicts of interest with other class members and will, along 

4  with counsel, vigorously litigate on the class’s behalf); see also Jaeger Decl. at ¶¶ 2–7, 
5  Ex. C to Berman Decl. (docket no. 28-3) (explaining that Jaeger works as the president of

7  during the class period, is strongly motivated to litigate vigorously and efficiently to 
8  maximize the recovery for himself and the putative class, and understands the important 

9  role of a lead plaintiff).  Accordingly, Jaeger is the presumptively “most adequate 
10  plaintiff.”                                                              
11      The remaining Movants do not oppose Jaeger’s appointment as lead plaintiff.  
12  Switzer, Hackbarth, Danev, and AP7 filed notices of non-opposition, docket nos. 50, 45, 
13  41, and 49, respectively.  The Court treats these Movants’ notices of non-opposition as 

14  withdrawal of their motions for appointment as lead plaintiff.  Therefore, Switzer, 
15  Hackbarth, Danev, and AP7’s motions, docket nos. 24, 31, 33, and 34, are STRICKEN in 
16  part as moot.                                                            
17      McCormick filed a response, docket no. 51, conceding that he does not possess the 
18  largest financial interest and requesting that the Court appoint him as lead plaintiff if the 

19  other Movants are disqualified.  The Court treats McCormick’s response as a notice of 
20  non-opposition, and McCormick’s motion, docket no. 17, is STRICKEN in part as moot.   
21      Ambrose initially challenged Jaeger’s financial interest, see docket no. 53, but 
22  later filed a notice of non-opposition to Jaeger’s appointment, docket no. 55.  Ambrose 
1  no longer questions Jaeger’s estimated losses, but requests that the Court appoint him as 
2  co-lead plaintiff alongside Jaeger because Jaeger traded exclusively in non-voting Class 
3  C shares while he traded in voting Class A shares.  See Notice of Non-Opp’n (docket 

4  no. 55 at 3).  The claims brought against Defendants and the nature of the putative class 
5  members’ alleged damages do not support Ambrose’s request that the Court appoint co-
6  lead plaintiffs.  See Outerwall,
2017 WL 881382
, at *9 (“[T]he decision whether to 
7  appoint a co-lead plaintiff often turns on the existence of disparate sub-groups of 
8  plaintiffs in the putative class.”); Miller v. Ventro Corp., No. C01-01287, 2001 U.S. Dist.
9 LEXIS 26027
, at *33–38 (N.D. Cal. Nov. 28, 2001) (appointing co-lead plaintiffs to 
10  represent shareholders and bondholders when bondholders presented additional legal 
11  theories); In re CTI BioPharma Corp. Sec. Litig., No. C16-216,
2016 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 12
  119301, at *12 (W.D. Wash. Sept. 2, 2016) (declining to appoint co-lead plaintiffs for 
13  preferred and common stock); In re Juniper Networks, Inc. Sec. Litig.,
264 F.R.D. 584
, 

14  594 (N.D. Cal. 2009) (finding that courts regularly appoint purchasers of one type of 
15  security to represent purchasers of other types of securities when the purchasers’ interests 
16  align).                                                                  
17      Ambrose contends that Jaeger’s ownership of Class C shares might affect Jaeger’s 
18  decision-making at settlement or trial.  However, Ambrose’s speculation concerning 

19  Jaeger’s decision-making is insufficient.  Ambrose has not shown that Jaeger’s interests 
20  are separate or independent of the other shareholders’ interests.  All Movants raise the 
21  same claims against Defendants under the Exchange Act, and all allege that they suffered 
22  damages when Zillow’s stock price fell, regardless of whether their shares have voting 
1  rights.  Although Ambrose argues that Jaeger’s ownership of non-voting Class C shares 
2  might cause Jaeger to favor Class C shares over Class A shares, Ambrose has not 
3  established that the differences between Class A and C shares would affect the claims or 

4  damages in this case.  The Court concludes, therefore, that appointing co-lead plaintiffs is 
5  not necessary, and Ambrose’s motion, docket no. 20, is DENIED in part.   
6      Finally, the Movants have provided no reason to disturb Jaeger’s choice of 
7  counsel.  See 15 U.S.C. § 78u-4(a)(3)(B)(v) (“The most adequate plaintiff shall, subject 
8  to the approval of the court, select and retain counsel to represent the class.”); see also 

9  Cavanaugh, 306 F.3d at 734 (“While the appointment of counsel is made subject to the 
10  approval of the court, the [PSLRA] clearly leaves the choice of class counsel in the hands 
11  of the lead plaintiff.”).  Jaeger has selected Hagens Berman Sobol Shapiro LLP (“Hagens 
12  Berman”) as lead counsel.  Having reviewed the firm’s résumé, Ex. E to Berman Decl. 
13  (docket no. 28-5), the Court finds that Hagens Berman is qualified and experienced to 

14  serve as lead counsel for the putative class.  Thus, the Court approves Jaeger’s choice of 
15  lead counsel.
